system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with hepatitis C-related cirrhosis and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for observation following his second transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) procedure targeting residual tumors in liver segments VI/VII and VIII. The procedure was performed successfully via the right femoral artery, delivering doxorubicin-eluting beads to the tumor bed. Access to a suspected phrenic artery supply was attempted but not achieved due to contrast and radiation limits. The patient remained stable throughout, with no post-procedural pain, nausea, or fever. Liver enzymes rose mildly as expected, and blood counts showed a transient decline. He was discharged home on day two with instructions to monitor for post-embolization syndrome, continue all home medications—including nadolol, spironolactone, glyburide, aspirin, and pravastatin—and follow up with oncology and hepatology in four weeks for imaging and treatment assessment.
problems: Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Aortocoronary bypass status
Personal history of tobacco use
Esophageal varices without mention of bleeding
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Old myocardial infarction

patient was

sterile fashion.

right common
femoral artery was punctured using a micropuncture set.  A small 
skin incision

exchanged for a
___ wire, which was advanced under fluoroscopy into the 
aorta.  The needle

the sheath was

procedure.

the left
external iliac artery and the C2 was exchanged for a ___ 
catheter over
the wire.  The ___ catheter was used to access the celiac 
artery.  A
small contrast injection was made to confirm position.  A DynaCT 
rotational
angiogram with 3D reconstruction was performed. 
 
Angiography of the celiac axis and CHA demonstrated conventional 
hepatic
arterial anatomy and patency of the right and left hepatic 
arteries.  Blush
was seen along the lateral and inferomedial portion of a segment 
VIII lesion
that had previously undergone TACE.  Using a combination of a 
Renegade ___
microcatheter, double angled Glidewire, and Headliner, the right 
hepatic
artery was selected.  A segmental branch of the RHA was selected 
witha

dominant
lesion in segment VIII.  Embolization was performed of this 
branch with 30 mg

post-embolization

withdrawn and

beyond the

imaging
supplying two lesions in segments VII/VIII near the hepatic dome 
was selected.

hepatic artery.
Embolization was performed of this branch with 35 mg of 
doxorubicin-loaded
beads.  Tumor stain in the anterior segment VII/VIII lesions 
were seen during
chemoembolization.

artery supply

aorta or

artery
catheterization.  A right common trunk adrenal artery arising 
directly from

arteriogram of

supplying the
upper renal pole, the next supplying the adrenal gland, and 
fianlly, a
take-off an intercostal branch.  The intercostal branch coursed 
cephalad and

two 3 mm x 2

After completion of chemoembolization, all wires and catheters

manual

procedure well and

lesion.

kidney and

bland
embolization to the segment of artery supplying residual tumor

VIII.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Hepatocellular carcinoma status post prior TACE x 2.  Repeat
TACE.

COMPARISONS:  Prior chemoembolization of ___.  Abdominal MRI of ___.

OPERATORS:  Dr. ___ (attending), Dr. ___ (fellow), Dr.
___ (resident).  The attending was present throughout the procedure and
supervised.

MEDICATIONS:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of
100 mcg of fentanyl, 3 mg of Versed, and 30 mg of Toradol throughout the total
intraservice time of 2 hours and 30 minutes, during which the patient's
hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored by an independently trained
radiology nurse. 1% subcutaneous lidocaine for local anesthesia.  

CHEMOEMBOLIZATION:  65 mg intra-arterial doxorubicin-eluting beads (Oncozene
100 micron).

CONTRAST:  225 cc of IV Optiray contrast.

FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  96.7 minutes, 3105 mGy.

PROCEDURES
1.  Right common femoral arterial access.
2.  Celiac rotational arteriogram with cone beam CT.
3.  Selective catheterization and angiography of a lateral segment VIII
branch.
4.  Selective transarterial chemoembolization of segment VIII branch supplying
a dominant tumor.
5.  Selective catheterization and angiography of a segments VII/VIII branches.
6.  Selective transarterial chemoembolization of segment VII/VIII branches
supplying two smaller lesions seen on prior MRI.
7.  Selective catheterization and angiography of right adrenal/intercostal
branch supplying segment VIII tumor.
8.  Rotational arteriogram with cone beam CT of right adrenal/intercostal
branch.
9.  Coiling and bland embolization of right adrenal/intercostal branch
supplying segment VIII mass.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:

Following discussion of the risks, benefits, and alternatives to the
procedure, informed written patient consent was obtained.  The patient was
brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  A
pre-procedural timeout and huddle were performed per departmental protocol. 
The skin of the right groin was prepped and draped in a usual sterile fashion.
Using a combination of palpatory and fluoroscopic guidance, the right common
femoral artery was punctured using a micropuncture set.  A small skin incision
made.  The inner dilator and nitinol wire were removed and exchanged for a
___ wire, which was advanced under fluoroscopy into the aorta.  The needle
was exchanged for a 5 ___ ___ Tip sheath.  The sidearm of the sheath was
continuously flush with heparinized saline throughout the procedure.

A C2 Cobra Glide catheter and ___ wire were used to access the left
external iliac artery and the C2 was exchanged for a Mikaelsson catheter over
the wire.  The Mikaelsson catheter was used to access the celiac artery.  A
small contrast injection was made to confirm position.  A DynaCT rotational
angiogram with 3D reconstruction was performed. 

Angiography of the celiac axis and CHA demonstrated conventional hepatic
arterial anatomy and patency of the right and left hepatic arteries.  Blush
was seen along the lateral and inferomedial portion of a segment VIII lesion
that had previously undergone TACE.  Using a combination of a Renegade ___
microcatheter, double angled Glidewire, and Headliner, the right hepatic
artery was selected.  A segmental branch of the RHA was selected witha
microwire and catheter that supplied the lateral portion of the dominant
lesion in segment VIII.  Embolization was performed of this branch with 30 mg
of doxorubicin eluted on to 100 micron beads (Oncozene) with post-embolization
arteriogram showing tumor staining.  The microcatheter was then withdrawn and
advanced into a separate second RHA segmental branch (distally beyond the
takeoff of the cystic artery). A segmental branch seen on prior imaging
supplying two lesions in segments VII/VIII near the hepatic dome was selected.
Tortuous arteries suggesting parasitized branches of the right hepatic artery.
Embolization was performed of this branch with 35 mg of doxorubicin-loaded
beads.  Tumor stain in the anterior segment VII/VIII lesions were seen during
chemoembolization.

While, based upon prior cross-sectional imaging, a right phrenic artery supply
was suspected, no right phrenic artery arising directly from the aorta or
celiac artery was identified on cone-beam CT or with attempts at artery
catheterization.  A right common trunk adrenal artery arising directly from
the aorta was accessed using a ___ catheter.  Rotational arteriogram of
this adrenal artery demonstrated three dominant branches, one supplying the
upper renal pole, the next supplying the adrenal gland, and fianlly, a
take-off an intercostal branch.  The intercostal branch coursed cephalad and
branches arising from this vessel supplied the medial aspect of the dominant
segment VIII tumor.  The microcatheter was advanced into the distal portion of
this artery (10-12 cm), beyond the branches supplying tumor and two 3 mm x 2
cm fibered coils were placed.  After contrast injection demonstrating no
contrast flow beyond the coils, bland embolization was performed of the
branches supplying tumor using 250 micron Embozene Microspheres to stasis.  

After completion of chemoembolization, all wires and catheters were removed. 
Hemostasis of the  right CFA access site was achieved using manual
compression.  No hematoma or evidence of swelling was present afterwards.  A
sterile dressing was applied.  The patient tolerated the procedure well and
there were no immediate post-procedure complication.

CONE-BEAM CT:  Two separate rotational angiography cone beam CTs were
performed, each with multiplanar and 3D volumetric reconstructions performed
at an independent workstation under the direct supervision of the attending
physician (Dr. ___.  The first cone-beam CT was essential in evaluating the
extent of residual tumor (particularly in Segment VIII, and area not well
assessed on recent MRI), to determine if newer areas of tumor had developed in
the interim since the last study, and was critical in outlining that the
various intrahepatic supply to the residual tumor, and in excluding supply to
the posteriomedial portion of the Segment VII tumor.  The second cone-beam CT
from the right common trunk adrenal-intercostal artery, was also essential in
evaluating the extent of residual tumor supplied by this branch in Segment VII
(not well-evaluated on either the prior MRI or first cone-beam CT).  This was
critical in determining that there was continuity with an intercostal branch
that subsequently required coil embolization to prevent non-target
embolization.   As noted above, these images were used in the interpretation,
decision making for intervention, and reporting of this procedure.

FINDINGS:
1. Conventional hepatic arterial anatomy. Prominent dorsal pancreatic artery
noted.
2. Initial fluoroscopic images demonstrated residual lipiodol from prior TACE
to a Segment VIII mass.
3. Cone-beam CT and celiac angiography identified two segmental RHA branches,
one supplying the Segment VIII mass, and the other supplying Segment VII/VIII
masses in the dome of the liver.  These were successfully sequentially
selected and TACE'ed with 85% of the DEB-TACE dose.  Care was taken to avoid
the cystic artery, which arises from the RHA.
4. Post-embolization staining of lateral portion of segment VIII lesion. 
Post-embolization staining in two segment VII/VIII lesions.
5. No definite supply from a right inferior phrenic was identified.  On review
of the cone-beam CT and prior cross-sectional imaging, a right common adrenal
trunk was identified that gave branches to the upper pole of the kidney and
right adrenal gland, before giving off an intercostal branch.  Several
arterial feeders were identified arising from the midportion of the
intercostal branch.  Selective distal catheterization and coil embolization
was performed to prevent non-target embolization, followed by bland
embolization to the segment of artery supplying residual tumor in Segment
VIII.   
6. Post-embolization staining in the medial segment VIII lesion. 

IMPRESSION: Successful right common femoral artery approach transarterial
chemoembolization of a dominant segment VIII lesion as well as two smaller
lesions anteriorly in segments VII/VIII.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You’re here today for your third TACE procedure for the liver tumors. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m doing okay, a bit nervous. The last two went fine, but I just hope this one helps stop the cancer from growing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. The MRI before this showed some remaining active tumor in segments VII and VIII, so we’re targeting those areas again today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they use the same treatment as last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll use doxorubicin-loaded beads to deliver chemotherapy directly to the tumors. We also saw a tricky blood vessel from the adrenal area feeding part of the tumor, so we’ll block that with coils to prevent damage to other areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Coils? Like metal ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Tiny coils, about the size of a small paperclip, to block off that side branch. It’s a safety step so the chemo only goes where we want it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. And the groin — will that hurt after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We access the artery through your right groin. You’ll have a small bandage, and we’ll ask you to lie flat for a few hours after to prevent bleeding. Some soreness is normal, but we’ll give you pain medicine if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The procedure is done, and it went very well. We treated the main tumor in segment VIII and two smaller ones near the top of your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel much during it. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were given light sedation. Most patients don’t feel pain during the procedure. We used imaging to guide everything precisely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did you find the vessel you were worried about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did. It came from the adrenal artery and branched into an intercostal vessel feeding the tumor. We placed coils and then used microspheres to block it. That should reduce the risk of the tumor getting blood from that route.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might have some low-grade fever, mild pain, or nausea over the next few days — that’s called post-embolization syndrome. Take acetaminophen for fever or pain, but no more than 2,000 mg a day. We’ll monitor your liver numbers too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable. No signs of infection or liver failure. We’re planning to discharge you in a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Should I restart all my usual meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue everything — your glyburide, spironolactone, nadolol, and the others. We’re sending prescriptions for ranitidine for 30 days and prochlorperazine in case you feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when do I see the liver doctor again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with hepatology and oncology in four weeks. They’ll order a new MRI to see how the tumors are responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get a fever at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A low fever is expected. But if it goes above 101, or you have severe pain, vomiting, or confusion, go to the ER. Those could be signs of infection or liver issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well today. Rest, stay hydrated, and we’ll see how you’re doing at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you’re feeling well, no pain, no nausea, and your groin site looks okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all good. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with hepatitis C-related cirrhosis and multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for observation following his third transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) procedure targeting residual tumors in liver segments VI, VII, and VIII. The procedure was successfully performed via the right femoral artery, delivering doxorubicin-eluting beads to the tumor sites. A previously suspected phrenic artery supply was not identified, but a feeding vessel from the right adrenal/intercostal artery was successfully coiled and embolized to prevent non-target perfusion. The patient tolerated the procedure well, with no immediate complications, pain, or bleeding at the access site. He remained stable throughout the admission, with mild expected changes in liver enzymes. He was discharged home the following day with instructions to monitor for post-embolization syndrome, continue all home medications, and follow up with oncology and hepatology in four weeks for imaging and treatment reassessment.
